transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-24 15:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Michael Rivera (CTO, Atlas), Sana Patel (ML Eng), Jamal Thompson (Platform)

Summary: quick sync on Dedicated sizing results from last week's run, discussing autoscale policies, burst planning, and next steps for the pilot. Some noise/typos in transcript, a few misrecognitions (KV cash, etc.).

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about 45 minutes, quick agenda — recap last week's benchmark, sizing tweaks, autoscale and burst, then next steps.
00:18 Michael Rivera: yeah thanks Alex, appreciate it. we ran the litmus load against the Dedicated pool last thursday as discussed. saw some good throughput, but we had a couple of tail latency spikes that worried the product team.
00:33 Priya Shah: cool can you give the numbers you have? average tokens/sec, p95, p99?
00:42 Sana Patel: sure — so baseline: single GPU we saw steady-state token throughput of ~18k tokens/minute for our model (that's MPT variant), p95 latency around 220ms, p99 around 480ms under our 1k concurrent sessions emulation. during a synthetic burst (sudden 3x request ramp) p99 jumped to 1.2s and some requests retried.
01:10 Alex Chen: thanks, that matches some of what we saw — the Dedicated pool was configured with min=2 gpus, target=4, max=8 for the test run and autoscale cool-down set to 90s. We saw scaling to 6 GPUs after about 45-60s of sustained higher queue depth.
01:28 Jamal Thompson: we noticed the scaling worked but initial fill — like when new workers spin up — caused a cold-start tail. is there a way to pre-warm or maintain a small burst buffer?
01:40 Priya Shah: yep — common pattern is to use a burst buffer/prefill policy: keep a tiny warm fraction (eg 1 extra GPU in idle warm state) and allow instant burst capacity via cold-start optimization. Also use prefetch of KV-cache for expected prefixes to reduce first-token latency. note: KV cache got transcribed as "KV cash" earlier, ignore that.
02:05 Michael Rivera: our main ask is predictable p95 under 300ms. p99 we can tolerate to 600-800ms but p95 is important. Also cost is a constraint — we can't keep a lot of warm GPUs 24/7.
02:20 Alex Chen: understood. tradeoff is pretty standard: keep min nodes for baseline QPS and configure rapid scale-up for bursts with short cool-downs but pre-warm policy. we can also set a burst budget: allow up to X GPU-hours per day for burst to reduce steady cost.
02:40 Sana Patel: can you explain how the burst budget works with autoscale? if it exceeds the budget, what happens?
02:50 Priya Shah: burst budget is rate-limited in our control plane — once you exhaust the daily burst quota, new scale-ups either get queued or fall back to a cheaper model variant (we automated model fallbacks in the last run to a quantized 4-bit variant). fallback policy kept tail latency but reduced cost. we can set a policy to not fall back for critical traffic.
03:16 Jamal Thompson: how about the startup time for new workers — 45 to 60 seconds seems high for the use-case; can we reduce to 20-30s?
03:25 Priya Shah: startup time depends on image pull, model load time, and compilation/quant kernel warm-up. for our test cluster we saw image caching on dedicated nodes, but model loading took ~18-25s per GPU. a few optimizations: use model precompiled artifacts, keep lightweight checkpoint in host memory, and enable warm-container pool which reduces cold start near 20-25s. fully getting to sub-20s is tough for large models without keeping them resident.
04:00 Michael Rivera: what about batching? we can't increase latency by batch windows, but small batching helps throughput. do you auto-adjust batching?
04:12 Alex Chen: yes Redwood Optimize can recommend batching thresholds; in serving runtime we do continuous batching with adaptive windows — we limit max window to keep p95 SLA. For you we set conservative max batch of 8 and adaptive min to 1. that gave better throughput with small P95 impact.
04:40 Sana Patel: during the burst test, we saw a queue backlog for ~30s before scale kicked in, causing the p99 spike. is that queue backlog in Redwood runtime or our load generator?
04:52 Priya Shah: that backlog correlates with the autoscale polling interval + cooldown. our autoscaler checks metrics every 10s and evaluates scale actions; we used a 90s cooldown so it prevented immediate re-scaling. for this workload i'd recommend lowering cooldown to 30s and using a short grace period to avoid flapping.
05:18 Jamal Thompson: if we lower cooldown to 30s, won't we risk oscillation and cost increase?
05:25 Alex Chen: you can mitigate oscillation by using a smoothed metric (moving average) plus a separate burst signal that triggers transient scale over the smoothed baseline. that way you get quick burst capacity for short spikes without repeatedly scale up/down cycles.
05:45 Michael Rivera: what about pre-warming cache for common prefixes? we have pretty predictable prompts for triage flows.
05:53 Priya Shah: good candidate for prefix caching — Redwood can prefill KV cache on warm nodes for a set of expected prompts. this shaves first-token time dramatically. we typically recommend profiling top 50 prefixes and pre-warming them in the warm pool.
06:12 Sana Patel: do you have any numbers on cost delta between keeping 2 warm GPUs vs letting autoscale handle it?
06:20 Alex Chen: rough rule: keeping 1 extra GPU warm increases steady cost by ~25-30% depending on instance type, but can reduce burst cost and improve tail latency. the burst budget offsets peaks; net cost depends on burst frequency. we'll provide a tailored cost estimate after we see your 24h histogram.
06:40 Priya Shah: also consider mixed pool types — use smaller GPUs for baseline and allow burst to larger high-throughput GPUs. that can save cost while providing headroom. but compatibility depends on model quantization and kernel support.
07:02 Michael Rivera: during the test you mentioned fallback to a quantized variant. did that change response quality too much for product?
07:12 Alex Chen: in the automated test we set fallback to 4-bit quantized variant; quality regressed slightly on edge cases but for most triage templates it was acceptable. we can pin critical routes to never fallback and only use fallback for non-critical background work.
07:35 Jamal Thompson: security question — we'll need VPC peering + SAML SSO + audit logs before we move beyond pilot. can you confirm Redwood Private supports that?
07:45 Priya Shah: yes, Private and Dedicated both support VPC peering, SAML/SSO, and detailed audit logs. Redwood can share SOC2 docs and network diagrams. we'll add that to next steps.
08:00 Michael Rivera: good. one operational question: for burst capacity, is there an API we can call to request temporary capacity in case of emergency?
08:09 Alex Chen: we have an admin API for on-demand capacity requests; typically customers use it as a manual trigger alongside autoscale. we can give Jamal API keys scoped to emergency-only calls.
08:20 Sana Patel: about the load test next week, what should we expect in terms of measurement? we'd like to capture token throughput, p50/p95/p99, scale events, startup times, and queue depths.
08:31 Priya Shah: yes, that's the checklist — also capture kernel compilation times, model load times, and any model fallbacks. Redwood will instrument traces so you can correlate scale events and tail latencies.
08:46 Michael Rivera: are there any pitfalls you saw in our earlier test config? we used a 90s cooldown and max batch size of 16.
08:55 Priya Shah: 16 is a bit high given your p95 target; we recommend max batch 8. also cooldown 90s is long for short bursts — switch to 30s with a burst smoothing metric. and set a burst budget (for example allow 6 GPU-hours/day of burst).
09:15 Jamal Thompson: what telemetry do we need on our side? logs, metrics, traces?
09:20 Alex Chen: metrics (CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, request latencies), occasional debug logs for model loads, and traces for request path to correlate with scale events. Redwood will provide dashboards in Console and share the Prometheus endpoint for host metrics.
09:38 Sana Patel: quick clarification — you mentioned fallback priority by route. how do we configure that?
09:44 Priya Shah: in the route config you can set a list of model variants with priority and fallback conditions. e.g., route A: primary model -> fallback quantized -> fallback cheaper region. we can share a templated config.
10:00 Michael Rivera: awesome. can we talk about SLA behavior if Dedicated is at capacity? if we hit max GPU and still have queued requests what happens?
10:10 Alex Chen: by policy you can choose either to queue with backpressure (client-side retry) or auto-failover to hosted route or to fallback model. Redwood supports multi-tier fallbacks: same model variant in another region, quantized variant, or hosted Redwood API. We'll work with you to pick the correct behavior per route.
10:34 Jamal Thompson: in our compliance requirements, we prefer no traffic egress to other regions; so fallback to hosted is off the table for some routes. need to ensure fallbacks are region-local or quantized on-prem.
10:44 Priya Shah: noted — we can restrict fallback policies to region-local variants only.
11:00 Sana Patel: anything on autoscale hysteresis settings? you mentioned smoothing metrics earlier.
11:05 Priya Shah: yes use a 15s short-term metric for burst triggers + a 5m moving average for baseline. combine with a cooldown of 30s and a separate burst token bucket that replenishes slowly.
11:25 Michael Rivera: what's the plan for the 2-hour load test? sequence?
11:29 Priya Shah: we'll run steady-state for 45m at baseline QPS, then a 10-minute ramp to 3x for bursts repeated 3 times with 20m recovery windows. we'll capture scale events and look for queue backlogs.
11:48 Jamal Thompson: ok we'll open network access and provide service account. I'll coordinate with Alex after the call.
11:55 Alex Chen: perfect. last thing — cost modeling. we'll provide two scenarios: keep 2 warm GPUs vs keep 1 warm + burst budget. You'll have numbers for steady 24h and expected monthly.
12:10 Michael Rivera: great. timeline? when can we expect configs and cost numbers?
12:16 Alex Chen: configs by 3/26, cost numbers same day, load test script by Priya by 3/28.
12:25 Sana Patel: fine. any blockers on our side? Jamal?
12:28 Jamal Thompson: just the VPC peering approvals and the firewall rules, should be done by 3/27.
12:36 Alex Chen: thanks everyone — recap in final minute: I'll send Dedicated sizing + autoscale template, SOC2/doc links, cost estimates. Priya sends load test and will run it with Jamal next week. Sana share traffic histograms.
12:52 Michael Rivera: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
